blocks.text: The Two-Week Deadline
Your boss just dropped this: "We need to launch the new website in two weeks. Can you put together a plan?" Two weeks. A whole website launch. Where do you even start?
The Blank Planning Document

You open a fresh doc to start planning. The cursor blinks. Your mind races through dozens of tasks, but nothing's organized yet.

Pretty stressful situation, isn't it?
In these circumstances, you would probably:

• Spend an hour brainstorming every possible task
  • Copy a plan from a previous project (that might not fit)
  • Google "website launch checklist" and adapt it
  • Schedule a meeting to figure it out somehow
All of these take time you don't always have. So, let's try something faster.

blocks.text: What happens next with your text plan: you paste it into a doc or email. Day 1 goes great — everyone knows their role. But:

• By Day 5, someone asks: "Wait, who's handling the SEO tests?"
  • By Day 9, deadlines have shifted, but the doc hasn't been updated.
  • By Day 12, nobody's sure what's actually done and what's still pending.
Text plans are great for thinking. Terrible for tracking.
ChatGPT is excellent at creating plans — but plans need to become trackable workflows, and that requires a visual tool. This is where Asana comes in.
blocks.title: The Gap Between Planning and Tracking

blocks.text: Meet Asana

Asana is a project management tool that turns text plans into visual, trackable timelines.

It's like a bridge between "here's the plan" and "here's how we're actually doing."
But while there are many project tools out there, why Asana? Three reasons:

1. It lets you visualize your timeline, no complex setup needed.
  2. It's easy to adopt.
  3. It works perfectly with ChatGPT, thanks to Asana's structure (tasks, owners, dates).
The bottom line: Asana strikes a balance between power and simplicity — robust enough for complex projects, yet simple enough to set up in 10 minutes.
What Asana Does

• Turns tasks into cards you can move and update
  • Shows who owns each task and when it's due
  • Displays everything on a timeline so you see the full picture
  • Updates automatically when things change
  • Keeps the whole team synced without endless status meetings
You get your ChatGPT plan, then bring it to life in Asana, where everyone can view and take action on it.
Now, let's see how you can turn your website launch plan into an Asana project.
Step 1: Create and Populate the Project

1. Click the Create button → Project → Blank project.
  2. Name it "Website Launch" → Create project.
  3. Click Add task and enter each task from your ChatGPT plan.
  4. For each task, click to assign an owner and set a due date.
Your project now has all tasks with owners and deadlines.
Step 2: Switch to Timeline View

1. Click Timeline at the top of your project.
  2. Your tasks now appear as bars across a calendar.
  3. Drag any bar to adjust dates.
After that, your 2-week plan will be interactive and you'll be able to see everything on it.
ChatGPT + Asana Together
Now let's see how these tools work as a team. You've got your plan in Asana, but what if you need to make adjustments to it?

Let's say your stakeholder just added a new requirement: "We need to include a blog section with three initial posts."

blocks.text: The Overloaded Designer

Imagine this: it's Thursday afternoon. Your designer, Maya, just messaged: "I don't think I can hit Friday's deadline. I still have six tasks due tomorrow." You check the project board. She's right — and you had no idea she was so busy. What can you do now?
The Invisible Overload

What happened: everyone on your team was working, tasks were getting assigned, and nobody realized Maya had way more on her plate than anyone else.

By the time she spoke up, it was almost too late.
This happens all the time in project management:

• Tasks get assigned as they come up (not strategically)
  • Some people say "yes" too often and get overloaded
  • Others have lighter loads, but you don't notice
  • Problems surface only when someone misses a deadline
You can't balance what you can't see.
Today, you'll learn how to see everyone's workload at a glance, spot the imbalance before it becomes a crisis, and redistribute tasks before anyone burns out.
Viewing Team Workload
Remember Asana from the last lesson? It doesn't just track tasks — it shows you who's carrying too much. Let's see how.

In your Asana project, you've assigned tasks to team members with due dates. Now you need to see the full picture.

How to view workload:

1. Open your project in Asana.
  2. Click Workload at the top (next to Timeline).
You now see each team member with their tasks displayed as capacity bars. Each person's bar indicates the number of hours or tasks assigned to them.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Workload view shows capacity, not productivity. Maya being busy while James has a light load means tasks need to be redistributed.

blocks.text: The Surprise That Wasn't

Two weeks before launch, your developer discovers the payment gateway doesn't work with your new platform. Complete integration rewrite needed.

Launch delays six weeks. Budget doubles. Stakeholders furious.

The worst part? This was predictable.
The "Surprise" Problem
Most project disasters aren't surprises — they're risks nobody bothered to list.
What typically happens:

• You focus on the plan (what should happen)
  • You don't think through what could go wrong
  • Small risks grow quietly in the background
  • By the time they surface, it's too late to prevent them
You can't mitigate risks you haven't identified.

feedbackCorrect.text: Exactly! Early risk identification gives you time to prevent or prepare — not just react.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Waiting until problems emerge means you're firefighting instead of preventing. Identify risks early when solutions are easier.

options.label: During the project, as issues come up, to avoid wasting time on problems that didn't happen
At the very beginning, before they become problems

blocks.question: When's the best time to identify project risks?

blocks.text: That's what we're building today! A way to spot risks before they happen, track which ones matter most, and have mitigation plans ready before anything goes wrong.

1. Open Notion and create a new page titled "Project Risk Tracker."
  2. Type /table and select Table — Database.
  3. Rename the default "Name" column to Risk.

  4. Transfer the plan to the respective "Mitigation Plan" cell.

Building a Weekly Risk Review
Your risk tracker is live. Now you need a habit to keep it useful.
Here's a simple Friday afternoon routine (10 minutes):

1. Open your Notion risk tracker.
  2. Filter to show Status = "Monitoring" or "Mitigating."
  3. For each active risk, ask: "Did anything change this week?"
  4. Update the Status if risks are resolved or escalated.
  5. Add new risks that emerged during the week.
  6. Assign owners to any unassigned risks.
Result: your tracker stays current, and you catch emerging risks early.

blocks.text: Stop Repeating Yourself

Project managers spend hours every week answering the same questions: "What was decided?" "Who's doing what?" "What's the status?"

The problem isn't your team — it's that information lives in your head, not in a system everyone can access. Let's fix team communication once and for all!
The Communication Black Hole

The usual pattern: you have meetings, make decisions, assign tasks. Then everyone forgets or interprets differently.

By Wednesday, half the team is confused. By Friday, you're re-explaining everything.
This happens because:

• Meeting notes are messy or incomplete
  • Updates live in your head, not written down
  • People miss meetings and never catch up
  • No single source of truth for "what's happening"
You can't align a team that doesn't have the same information.

feedbackCorrect.text: That's right! It's not about attention — it's about having a consistent system to capture and share what matters.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Complexity isn't the issue. Even complex projects can be summarized clearly if you have a clear system in place.

blocks.text: Meet Slack for Team Updates
Slack is your team's communication hub — where conversations, updates, and decisions already happen.
Why Slack Works for Communication

• Everyone's already there — no need to check another tool
  • Channel organization: #project-updates for announcements, #general for casual chat
  • Threaded system: the team can ask questions directly under your update
  • Search and pins help simple info discovery
The bottom line: posting summaries in Slack means 100% visibility with zero extra effort from your team.
Posting Updates in Slack
Now, let's share your summary with the team in Slack:

1. Copy your summary from ChatGPT.
  2. Open Slack and go to your project channel (e.g., #project-alpha).
  3. Paste the summary into the message box.
  4. Add a quick intro line like: "Quick recap from today's sprint planning:" and click Send.
Optional: click the pin icon to keep it at the top of the channel for easy reference.

feedbackCorrect.text: Right on spot! Posting while memory is fresh means faster clarification if someone is confused — context is still active.

feedbackIncorrect.text: The sooner you post, the easier it is for people to ask follow-up questions while everyone still remembers the discussion.

blocks.text: Understanding the Difference

By specifying sections (completed, in progress, blockers, priorities), you transformed a paragraph dump into a scannable report.

Same information. Completely different usability.
However, there's a better way than typing that detailed prompt every week. Create one reusable reporting prompt — and use it forever. Save it as a template on your computer for quick access.
Creating Your Reusable Report Template
Let's build a reporting prompt you can use every single week with zero modification!

"Turn these project updates into a professional weekly summary with these sections:
  • Completed this week: finished tasks with owner names
  • In progress: current work with % complete or due dates
  • Blockers & risks: issues and mitigation plans
  • Next week's priorities: top 3-5 focus areas
Updates: *paste your notes here*"
blocks.title: Your Reusable Reporting Prompt

blocks.text: How to Use It

1. Save this prompt in a doc or note. Every Friday, copy the prompt.
  2. Replace *paste your notes here* with your scattered updates.
  3. ChatGPT generates your formatted report.

Now every weekly report has the same professional structure. Your stakeholders know exactly where to look for blockers, completed work, or next steps.

Consistency builds trust.

blocks.text: The Trust Problem

Your team starts using AI for project updates. Stakeholders love the efficiency. Then someone asks: "Wait, did you write this report or did AI?"

Suddenly, there's doubt. Are decisions actually yours? Is sensitive data safe? Who's accountable if something goes wrong?

You need answers.
The Invisible Risk
AI tools are powerful, but using them without guidelines creates problems you don't see coming.

feedbackCorrect.text: The real risks are data leaks, unverified outputs, and misplaced trust. Guidelines prevent all three!

feedbackIncorrect.text: Using AI for everything isn't the core risk — misuse is. The danger is sharing sensitive data, skipping verification, or blindly trusting outputs. Guidelines create safe boundaries.

feedbackCorrect.text: You're right! Your policy needs to clearly define boundaries, including data safety, verification requirements, and accountability — not permissions or technical details.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Policies aren't about limiting access or explaining technology — they're about safe usage boundaries for everyone.

feedbackCorrect.text: Right on target! Sensitive data (client info, financials, personal details) needs protection. AI tools can't guarantee privacy. And, without guidelines, people don't know what data is safe to share with AI.

feedbackIncorrect.text: The risk isn't accuracy — it's privacy. Confidential data should never leave your secure systems. And, without guidelines, people don't know what data is safe to share with AI.

blocks.text: Now that you know why guidelines matter and what they need to address, let's actually look at how they are created.
What to Include in Your AI Policy

• Data privacy: what information you can/can't share with AI
  • Human review: which outputs need verification before use
  • Transparency: when to disclose that AI was used
  • Accountability: who's responsible if AI makes a mistake
  • Appropriate use: what tasks fit AI vs. require human judgment
These five areas prevent the most common AI risks.

feedbackCorrect.text: Exactly. External, high-stakes communication (especially with numbers) needs verification. Internal formatting — less critical.

feedbackIncorrect.text: High-stakes external content needs human review. Internal team updates have lower risk and can move faster.

blocks.text: Storing Your Policy in Notion
Let's make your AI policy accessible to everyone who needs it.

1. Open Notion and create a new page titled "AI Usage Guidelines."
  2. Paste your ChatGPT policy into the page.
  3. Add a "Table of Contents" block at the top (type /toc) for easy navigation.
  4. Use "Toggle" blocks (type /toggle) for each section so people can expand what they need.
  5. Add it to your team's workspace sidebar for quick access.
  6. Share the page link in your team Slack channel.
Now your policy is:

• Accessible 24/7 in your shared workspace
  • Searchable (team can instantly find answer to their questions like "Can I share client data?")
  • Easy to update as tools and needs evolve
